title: The arrows (1 Samuel 20)
hookLine: Jonathan signals with arrows, and the friends part in tears

cards: A code, worked out in advance between two friends who can't risk being seen talking. David will hide in a field, beside a stone.
Jonathan will come out as if for target practice, with a boy to fetch his arrows, and shoot three arrows to the side. If he shouts that the arrows are on this side of you, David is safe: come home.
If he shouts that they're beyond you, the king means to kill him: go. Jonathan has to find out which at his father's table, at the feast of the new moon.
Then he must say it aloud, in front of a boy who has no idea what it means.

teach.b: At the feast, David's seat is empty. On the second day Saul asks, and Jonathan covers for his friend. Saul explodes.
He shames his own son, tells him that as long as David lives, Jonathan's kingdom won't stand, and throws a spear at him.
Now Jonathan knows. In the morning he goes out to the field. The boy runs, Jonathan shoots past him, and calls the line they agreed on: "Behold, the arrows are beyond thee."
The answer is go. Then he adds, as if to a slow servant: make speed, hurry, don't stay. The words are for the boy, and for the man behind the stone.
And here the plan breaks down, in the best way.
The code was built so they wouldn't have to meet. Jonathan sends the boy back to town with his weapons. David comes out and bows to the ground.
They kiss and weep together, and the text says David wept the more. Jonathan's last words are a blessing and a promise: go in peace.
We have sworn in the name of the Lord that the Lord will be between me and you, and between my children and your children, for ever. He doesn't say goodbye by signal, or by pretending it's fine.
He sends the witness away and says it face to face.
The arrows told David everything he needed to know.
The goodbye told him something the arrows couldn't.

how: Jews read the parting of David and Jonathan in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets; the chapter's feast of the new moon, Rosh Chodesh, is still marked in the Jewish calendar.

o: a test of David's skill as an archer
Jonathan's signal telling David to flee
a sign that Saul's anger had passed

p: David's place at the new moon feast

s: Saul threw a spear at Jonathan
when Jonathan covered for David at the feast, Saul threw a spear at his own son.
the friends parted by signal and never met
Jonathan sent the boy back to town, and David came out. they kissed and wept together.
the text says the boy knew nothing; only Jonathan and David knew the matter.

games.q: you're Jonathan. the arrows have told David to run, and the boy is standing beside you. what do you do?
o: walk home and let the signal be the goodbye.
send the boy away, so you and David can meet.
games.why: he sends the boy back to town with his weapons. David comes out, and they weep together before Jonathan says go in peace.

practice: Let someone come to mind who's leaving, or whom you're leaving, a goodbye that keeps getting done by text or not at all.
Think what you'd want to say face to face, the way Jonathan sent the boy away to say it; one sentence is enough. If you pray, you can hold Jonathan's words: go in peace.

wordCard.voice: The arrows. A signal shot past a boy in a field, that told David to go, and a goodbye said in person anyway. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the arrows, the signal Jonathan shoots past the boy in 1 Samuel 20.

carryVoice: Your line: the arrows are beyond thee. Some goodbyes need a face, not a signal. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: Behold, the arrows are beyond thee
